11970:
Permission is the act of someone in authority allowing another person to do something.

It's not just any kind of agreement — it specifically involves two things:

  1. An authority — someone who has the power to say yes or no.
  2. A request or action — something that requires that authority's approval before it can happen.

When you have permission, it means the person with authority has said: "Yes, you may do this."

When you don't have permission, doing that thing would be considered wrong, prohibited, or at least inappropriate.

A child asks a parent: "Can I stay up late tonight?" The parent says yes. The child now has permission to stay up late.

Without the parent's permission, staying up late would go against the rules. That's the key: permission exists in situations where someone has the right to control whether an action is allowed or not.

Permission works both as an uncountable noun and, in some contexts, as a countable noun. This is important to understand.

As an uncountable noun (most common use)

When talking about the general concept of being allowed to do something, "permission" has no article ("a/an") and no plural form.

  • "You need permission to enter this building."
  • "She left without permission."
  • "Do I have your permission to speak?"
  • "He was granted permission to work abroad."

Here, permission refers to the state of being allowed — it's an abstract concept, like "freedom" or "knowledge."

As a countable noun (specific, formal use)

In legal, official, or technical contexts, you will sometimes see "a permission" or "permissions" (plural). Here, it refers to a specific, defined right that is granted.

  • In computers and software: "This app is requesting permissions to access your camera and contacts." — Each permission is a specific right (access to camera = one permission; access to contacts = another).
  • In law and official documents: "The necessary permissions were obtained before construction began." — Each official permit or authorization is counted as one permission.

So when permission is tangible, documented, or specific and countable, it can take a plural or article.
What Makes "Permission" Different from Similar Words

Learners often confuse permission with several related words. Understanding the differences sharpens your understanding of what permission really means.

Permission vs. Consent
Both involve allowing something, but consent is more personal and more about agreeing from your own free will, especially in sensitive situations (medical procedures, personal relationships). Permission is broader and more authority-based.

  • A patient gives consent to surgery.
  • A student gets permission from a teacher to leave class.

Permission vs. Authorization
Authorization is a more formal, often official version of permission. It usually involves an institution, a document, or a system — not just a person's word.

  • A manager gives permission for you to leave early.
  • A government authorizes a company to operate in a particular industry.

Permission vs. Approval
Approval is wider — it can mean simply thinking something is good, or agreeing with it in principle. Permission is specifically about allowing an action to take place.

  • A boss approves of your idea (she thinks it's good).
  • A boss gives permission for you to go ahead with the idea (she allows you to act).

Permission vs. License
A license is a formal, usually written and official form of permission — often granted by a government or regulatory body.

  • A driver's license = official permission from the government to drive.
  • Saying "I have permission to drive" is informal and personal.
  • Saying "I have a license to drive" means there is a formal document proving that permission.

Permission vs. Leave
In formal, military, or official language, "leave" means permission to be absent from your duties or post.

  • "The soldier was granted leave for two weeks." (= he had official permission to be away)
  • In everyday British English, you might hear: "May I take leave to address this matter?" (= may I have permission to…)

Something worth really internalizing: permission implies a power difference.

The person who gives permission has some form of authority, control, or ownership over the situation. The person who receives permission is in a position where they must defer to that authority.

This is why you ask a landlord for permission to make changes to an apartment — they own it, so they control what happens to it.

This is also why, in professional settings, asking for permission is sometimes seen as empowering the other person over you — and why experienced professionals might instead say: "I'm planning to do X unless you have any objections," rather than "Do I have your permission to do X?"

Understanding this dimension helps you use and interpret the word with social precision.
Common Verb Collocations (how "permission" is used with verbs)

These are the most natural and widely-used pairings:

  • Ask for / seek permission — to make a request to be allowed to do something.
  • Get / obtain / receive permission — to successfully be allowed.
  • Give / grant / extend permission — the authority allows the action.
  • Deny / refuse / withhold permission — the authority says no.
  • Have permission — to currently be in a state of being allowed.
  • Need / require permission — the situation demands authorization.
  • Give someone permission to do something — the most natural full structure.

"You must seek permission from the board before proceeding."
"She was denied permission to publish the photographs."
"I have permission to access the restricted area."

• with permission — "The excerpt is reproduced with permission from the publisher." (meaning: it was allowed)
  • without permission — "He used the image without permission." (meaning: he had no right to)
  • by permission of — formal way of saying someone allowed it: "Performed by permission of the composer."
  • with your permission — a polite phrase meaning "if you allow me to": "With your permission, I'd like to raise a different point."
  • permission to do something — the standard structure: "permission to leave," "permission to speak."

In formal, legal, or official writing, permission is used in full, careful phrases:

  • "Written permission must be obtained prior to reproduction."
  • "No construction may commence without planning permission."

In everyday speech, people often use lighter alternatives:

  • Instead of "May I have permission to…", people say: "Is it okay if I…?" or "Can I…?"
  • "Mom, can I go to the park?" is asking for permission — even though the word itself isn't used.

Knowing this helps you recognize when permission is being asked for or given, even when the word "permission" doesn't appear.
A Few Important Phrases Worth Knowing

• Permission slip — a physical or digital document (common in schools) that a parent signs to allow their child to participate in an activity. "Bring back your signed permission slip by Friday."
  • Without so much as asking permission — an idiom meaning someone acted boldly without asking anyone. "She rearranged the entire office without so much as asking permission."
  • Tacit permission — permission that is implied or understood but never directly spoken or written. "By not objecting, the manager gave tacit permission for the team to proceed."
  • Blanket permission — broad permission that covers many situations at once, rather than needing to ask each time. "The author gave blanket permission for her essays to be used in educational settings."

Permission (noun) is the authorization or allowance given by someone with authority for another person to do something. It implies a relationship where one party controls access to an action, space, or resource, and another party must seek their approval. It is typically uncountable when referring to the general concept, and countable when referring to specific, formal rights (as in legal or technical contexts). It is obtained, granted, denied, or withheld — and its absence makes an action unauthorized or prohibited.
11971:
Permissive describes something or someone that allows a lot of freedom — that does not impose many rules, restrictions, or controls, and tends to say "yes" rather than "no."

The word is about permission. When something or someone is permissive, they readily give permission, or they create an environment where things are broadly allowed.

The word can describe people, environments, systems, cultures, and policies.

A permissive parent is one who gives their children a lot of freedom — they don't enforce strict rules, they let children make their own choices, and they rarely punish misbehaviour. The child can stay up late, eat what they want, and skip chores without consequences.

A permissive society is one that tolerates a wide range of behaviours and lifestyles without judging or restricting them. It doesn't impose a single standard of how people should live.

A permissive policy or law is one that grants broad freedoms rather than tight controls. A permissive gun law, for example, makes it easy to own or carry a weapon with few restrictions.

A permissive software licence (common in tech) is one that allows people to use, modify, and share the software with very few conditions attached.
The Spectrum: From Positive to Negative

This is an important nuance — permissive is not always a compliment, and not always a criticism. Its tone depends entirely on context and the speaker's viewpoint.

When used positively or neutrally:
It suggests open-mindedness, trust, flexibility, and respect for individual freedom. A permissive school environment might allow students to explore creatively without rigid rules crushing their curiosity.

When used critically:
It suggests a lack of necessary discipline or control — that someone or something is too lenient, to the point of being irresponsible. A critic might say a permissive parent is raising children who have no respect for boundaries because they've never been told "no."

So the same word can be a compliment ("this is a refreshingly permissive workplace — I can actually be myself") or a criticism ("the permissive attitude toward violence in media is harmful"), depending on who's speaking and what they value.

Something can be somewhat permissive (relaxed, flexible, easygoing) or very permissive (so loose that it borders on negligent or careless). The more permissive something is, the fewer restrictions it imposes — at the extreme end, it may impose none at all.

It helps to understand what it isn't:

  • It is not the same as "supportive." Being supportive means actively helping someone. Being permissive just means not stopping them.
  • It is not the same as "approving." A permissive parent may not approve of their child's choices — they simply don't intervene.
  • It is not the same as "weak" by definition, though people who dislike permissiveness often frame it that way.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Lenient is the closest synonym. Both mean "not strict." But lenient is almost always used for people (especially those in authority — a lenient judge, a lenient teacher) and usually in specific situations where punishment or discipline is expected but reduced. Permissive is broader — it describes a general attitude, culture, or system that allows freedom overall, not just in one moment.

Tolerant means willing to accept things you may personally disagree with. You can be tolerant without being permissive — you might disapprove of something but choose not to act against it. Permissive implies a more general openness or freedom, not just endurance of something disliked.

Liberal (in this sense, not political) means favouring freedom and less restriction. It overlaps heavily with permissive, but liberal leans more toward a philosophy or value system, while permissive focuses more on the practical result — the actual allowing of things.

Indulgent means giving someone what they want, often excessively. Indulgent carries a stronger sense of actively satisfying desires (spoiling a child with gifts), while permissive is more about not restricting them.

• "The company has a permissive work-from-home policy — employees can work wherever they like." (positive/neutral)
  • "Critics say the government's permissive approach to pollution has caused long-term damage." (negative)
  • "She grew up in a permissive household where she was rarely told what to do." (neutral — could be read either way)
  • "The permissive atmosphere at the festival meant people felt free to express themselves without judgment." (positive)
  • "The new rules are far more permissive than the old ones — almost anything is allowed now." (neutral)
Permissive means allowing a lot and restricting little — whether that's a good thing or a bad thing depends on what is being allowed, how much, and who you ask.
11972:
To permit something means to allow it to happen — but with an important layer: the person or thing permitting has the authority or power to say yes or no in the first place.

This is the heart of the word. You can only permit something if you have some control over whether it happens. A random stranger cannot permit you to enter a restricted building — only someone with authority over that building can.

1. A person (or rule) actively gives permission

This is the most common use. Someone with authority consciously decides to allow something.

The doctor permitted the patient to eat solid food again.
The school permits students to use their phones during lunch.
Her parents permitted her to stay out until midnight.

Notice the pattern here: someone permits someone else to do something. The person permitting has the power to say no — but chooses to say yes.

2. Circumstances or conditions make something possible

Here, no human authority is involved. Instead, a situation, condition, or factor "allows" something to happen by not blocking it.

If time permits, I will explain everything in detail.
Weather permitting, the match will be played on Saturday.
The small window permitted just enough light into the room.

In this sense, "permit" means the conditions are favorable enough for something to occur. Time, weather, space, light — these aren't people, but they can still "permit" or "not permit" things by being favorable or unfavorable.

Understanding how "permit" is grammatically used will help you use it correctly every time.

Pattern 1: permit + someone + to do something

The manager permitted the team to work from home.
The officer permitted us to pass.

Pattern 2: permit + doing something (a gerund)

The sign says: "No permit is given — the rules do not permit smoking here."
Company policy does not permit sharing confidential information.

Pattern 3: permit + a noun (a thing or action)

The ticket permits entry to all three floors.
The law permits this kind of agreement.

Pattern 4: circumstances + permit (no object)

I will call you back when time permits.
We will proceed, weather permitting.

"Permit" sits on the formal end of the spectrum. Compare:

  • "You can go." → casual
  • "You may go." → slightly formal
  • "You are permitted to go." → formal, often official or institutional

This is why you see "permit" frequently in legal writing, official rules, institutional policies, institutional notices, and formal speech. In everyday conversation between friends, people usually say let or allow instead.

✅ "The rules permit passengers to carry one bag." (formal, official)
✅ "She let me borrow her book." (casual)
✅ "He allowed me to leave early." (neutral)

All three mean roughly the same thing, but "permit" signals a more official or authoritative context.
The Key Underlying Idea: Authority + Consent

Every use of "permit" carries the idea that someone or something has the power to block an action, and is instead choosing not to block it. That's what makes "permit" different from simply "happen."

  • If rain falls, rain doesn't permit itself to fall — it just falls. No authority is involved.
  • But if a venue permits outdoor events despite a rainy forecast, a decision-maker with control over that venue is making a choice to allow it.

This is why we say "the law permits X" — because the law could have forbidden X, but instead it allows it.

The visa permits the holder to stay for 90 days.

(A document granting formal permission)

His poor health did not permit him to travel.

(His health conditions blocked travel — circumstances, not a person)

I would have stayed longer, but time did not permit it.

(Same idea — time as a limiting factor)

The referee permitted the game to continue despite the injury.

(An authority figure making a deliberate choice to allow something)

• It does not mean to force or make something happen.
  • It does not mean to encourage or approve of something morally. A government may permit something without endorsing it. Permitting is about legal or practical allowance, not moral praise.

"The country permits gambling" means gambling is legally allowed — not that the government thinks gambling is a great idea.

To permit something is to allow it, especially from a position of authority or control — whether that's a person granting permission, a rule that doesn't forbid something, or circumstances that make something possible.
11973: A permutation is a specific arrangement of things in a particular order. That's the core idea.

In general use, a permutation refers to one possible version of something — a particular way things can be ordered, arranged, or varied.

Imagine you're deciding the running order for three speakers at an event: Alice, Bob, and Carol. You could have Alice first, then Bob, then Carol. Or Bob first, then Carol, then Alice. Each distinct ordering is a permutation. If someone says "we've tried every permutation of the schedule," they mean they've gone through every possible way to arrange it.

In this sense, the word is used loosely to mean "variation" or "rearrangement." You'll often see it used in business, planning, or everyday conversation:

  • "The designers explored every permutation of the logo."
  • "There are countless permutations of this recipe depending on the ingredients you use."

The word carries a slight implication of systematic exhaustiveness — when someone uses the word permutation, they're often hinting that they're not just talking about one or two variations, but the full landscape of possibilities.

In mathematics, the word becomes very precise, and this is where you need to understand it most carefully.

A permutation is an ordered arrangement of items selected from a set, where the order in which the items appear fundamentally matters.

Take the three letters: A, B, C.

If you arrange all three, the possible permutations are:
ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA — that's 6 total arrangements.

These are all considered different permutations, even though they use the same three letters, because the order is different. ABC ≠ BAC in the world of permutations.

Now here's something important: permutations don't always involve arranging all the items in a set. You might only be arranging some of them. Say you have five people but only three chairs to seat them. You're choosing 3 people from 5 and the order of seating matters (chair 1, chair 2, chair 3 are distinct seats). Each possible outcome is a permutation.

The mathematical formula for this is nPr (read as "n permute r"), where:

  • n = the total number of items you're choosing from
  • r = how many items you're actually arranging

The formula is: nPr = n! / (n − r)!

The ! symbol means factorial — you multiply a number by every whole number below it down to 1. So 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120.

Using the chairs example: 5P3 = 5! / (5−3)! = 120 / 2 = 60 permutations.
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember: Order Matters

The defining feature of a permutation — the thing that separates it from its close cousin, the combination — is that order matters.

Think of a lock with a 3-digit code. The sequence 4-7-2 is completely different from 7-2-4, even though they use the same numbers. That's a permutation problem, because the order changes the outcome.

Now contrast this with a combination (the other key word you'll encounter alongside permutation): if you're choosing 3 pizza toppings from a menu, it doesn't matter whether you pick pepperoni first or mushrooms first — you still end up with the same pizza. Order is irrelevant. That's a combination.

A simple way to remember the difference:

  • Permutation → Position matters. (Like a podium: 1st, 2nd, and 3rd place are different.)
  • Combination → Position is ignored. (Like a fruit bowl: apples, oranges, bananas — the grouping is what counts, not the order.)
How the Word Is Used in a Sentence

As a noun, permutation can be used in both singular and plural forms:

  • "Each permutation of the password was tested by the hacker." (one specific arrangement)
  • "The number of permutations grew rapidly as we added more variables." (multiple possible arrangements)
  • "This is just one permutation of the plan; there are many others." (one version among several)

A permutation is an ordered arrangement of things. In everyday speech, it means a variation or rearrangement of something. In mathematics, it is the precise count or listing of all the ways you can arrange a selection of items when their order matters.

Whenever you hear or read the word, ask yourself: "Are we talking about different arrangements of the same things, where their order or sequence is what changes things?" If yes — you're in permutation territory.
11974:
Something is pernicious when it causes serious harm — but does so in a slow, subtle, and often hidden way. It doesn't announce itself. It quietly works against you, and by the time you notice the damage, it may already be severe or even irreversible.

Think of it this way: a punch to the face is harmful. But a slow-acting poison slipped into your drink is pernicious. Both cause harm — but pernicious harm creeps in quietly, often disguised or undetected, and the damage compounds over time.
What makes it different from just "harmful"

This is the most important thing to understand. Calling something "harmful" just tells you it causes damage. Calling something pernicious tells you how it causes damage — and that "how" is the whole point.

Something pernicious has three qualities working together:

It is genuinely harmful, not mildly unpleasant. There is real, serious damage involved. A slightly rude comment is not pernicious. A habit that slowly destroys your health is.

It is gradual and subtle. The damage builds slowly, quietly, over time. You might not feel it happening. Pernicious things rarely announce their harm upfront.

It is hard to detect or resist. Often, pernicious things appear normal, harmless, or even attractive at first. They spread easily because people don't immediately recognize them as dangerous.

This is precisely why writers and speakers choose the word "pernicious" instead of simply saying "bad" or "harmful." It is a loaded word. It carries the warning: this thing works in the shadows, quietly, and causes deep damage before you realize what's happening.

"The pernicious effects of misinformation took years to undo."
The false information spread quietly, sounded believable, and by the time people realised it was wrong, it had already shaped opinions and decisions on a large scale. Classic pernicious behaviour — subtle entry, serious damage.

"He was a pernicious influence on the younger students."
His influence didn't look obviously bad at first. But over time, he gradually led the younger students in a harmful direction. The damage was slow and subtle.

"Smoking is a pernicious habit."
It harms the body slowly. The damage is invisible for years. And by the time it shows up, it is serious. That pattern — gradual, hidden, devastating — is the essence of pernicious.

"The pernicious idea that success requires no effort ruined his discipline."
The idea sounded appealing (who doesn't want success without effort?). It spread subtly, without resistance. And slowly, it destroyed his work ethic. A classic pernicious idea.

"Social media can have pernicious effects on self-esteem, especially in teenagers."
Not every scroll session feels damaging. But over months and years, constant comparison quietly erodes how people see themselves. The harm is real, gradual, and hard to pinpoint — pernicious.

It is not used for sudden, violent, or immediate harm. A car crash is not pernicious — it is violent and instantaneous. Pernicious harm unfolds over time.

It is not used for things that are merely annoying or mildly bad. A noisy neighbour is not pernicious. A belief system that quietly radicalises someone over years is.

It is not used casually in everyday small talk. You would not say "that cold was pernicious" unless you are being deliberately dramatic. It is a word that carries weight, and it is used for things worthy of that weight.

In the real world, you will most often see "pernicious" paired with words like: influence, effects, habit, lie, myth, idea, belief, trend, doctrine, and impact. These pairings make sense — all of them are things that can spread quietly and do damage gradually.

One important special case: pernicious anemia is a specific medical condition in which the body cannot absorb vitamin B12 properly, leading to serious harm over time. The word was chosen deliberately in medicine because the condition is slow, hidden, and seriously damaging — exactly what pernicious means.
The formality and tone of the word

Pernicious is a formal, intellectual word. You will encounter it in essays, academic writing, literary fiction, journalism, speeches, and serious debate. It signals that the speaker or writer is making a deliberate, considered point — not just saying something is "bad," but specifically calling out the insidious, quietly destructive nature of something.

When someone uses this word, they want you to feel concerned in a particular way — not the sharp alarm of immediate danger, but the slow dread of something working against you that you might not even be aware of.
A memory trick to lock it in

Picture a quiet villain. Not the kind who announces their evil plans loudly — but the kind who works in the shadows, patiently, over years, causing devastating damage before anyone notices. No drama. No warning. Just slow, serious, hidden harm.

That quiet villain is pernicious. Anything that works that way — spreading damage gradually, subtly, seriously — deserves to be called pernicious.
11975:
To perorate means to speak at great length in a grand, formal, or pompous way — often to the point where the listener feels the speaker is going on far too long and enjoying the sound of their own voice a little too much.

Think of a politician who, instead of making a simple point, launches into a sweeping, dramatic, elaborate speech that stretches on and on — full of lofty language, big gestures, and soaring declarations. That politician is perorating.

This word carries two distinct but related meanings, and understanding both is important.

Meaning 1 — The more common, everyday use:
To speak at tedious, excessive, or pompous length. The tone here is slightly critical. When you say someone "perorated," you are gently (or not so gently) mocking them for overdoing it — for being long-winded and self-important in their speech.

The professor perorated for forty minutes about a topic that needed only five.

She perorated endlessly at dinner, lecturing everyone about a subject no one had asked about.

Meaning 2 — The formal, rhetorical use:
To deliver the conclusion of a formal speech — the closing, wrapping-up section where the speaker pulls everything together and ends with force. This is a technical sense borrowed from classical public speaking.

The senator perorated with a passionate call to action that brought the crowd to its feet.

In this sense, it does not carry the mocking tone — it simply means the speaker is delivering their grand finale.

The meaning you take from "perorate" often depends on who is saying it and how.

  • If a critic says a speaker "perorated," they almost certainly mean the speaker droned on pompously and self-indulgently.
  • If a speechwriter or debate coach says a speaker "perorated well," they likely mean the speaker delivered a powerful, well-crafted closing.

In modern everyday writing and conversation, Meaning 1 (long-winded and pompous) is far more common. When in doubt, that is the safe assumption.

"Perorate" has a formal, slightly elevated register — meaning you will encounter it more in essays, literary criticism, political commentary, and sophisticated journalism than in casual conversation. It is the kind of word a writer reaches for when they want to describe a speaker with a hint of dry wit or disapproval.

It also implies a performance quality — someone who perorates is not just talking; they are holding forth, as if on a stage, aware of an audience, relishing the spotlight.
How It Differs From Similar Words

• Ramble — to talk in a disorganized, wandering way. Rambling is messy. Perorating is grand and deliberate — it thinks it is impressive.
  • Lecture — to speak instructively, often in a one-sided way. Lecturing implies authority. Perorating implies showiness.
  • Orate — to make a formal speech. Neutral or positive in tone. Perorating is like orating but taken too far, or with excessive drama at the close.
  • Pontificate — the closest cousin. Both words describe pompous, self-important speech. "Pontificate" suggests someone speaking as if they are the ultimate authority. "Perorate" focuses more on the length, grandness, and theatrical quality of the speech.

——
Most common meaningTo speak at great, pompous, theatrical length
Secondary meaningTo deliver the grand closing of a formal speech
ConnotationSlightly mocking / critical (in common use)
Who uses itWriters, critics, commentators
Closest cousinPontificate
One Final Example to Tie It Together

Imagine a CEO addressing employees after a merger. A simple, direct CEO would say: "This merger will open new opportunities for all of us. Thank you." But a CEO who perorates would spend forty-five minutes weaving a grand narrative about the arc of history, the courage of visionaries, the destiny of the company — with dramatic pauses, soaring language, and a thunderous closing — leaving everyone exhausted and slightly bewildered.

That, in a nutshell, is what it means to perorate.
11976:
A peroration is the concluding section of a formal speech — the powerful ending where a speaker wraps everything up, reminds the audience of their key points, and makes one final push to move, persuade, or inspire them.

Think of it like the final chapter of a book, except it's spoken aloud, and it's deliberately crafted to leave a deep, lasting impression on the audience.
Breaking It Down a Little More

When a skilled speaker gives a formal speech — a politician rallying voters, a lawyer addressing a jury, a preacher delivering a sermon — they don't just stop talking when they run out of things to say. They build toward a deliberate, carefully constructed ending. That ending is the peroration.

A peroration typically does two things at once:

1. It summarizes. The speaker revisits the main arguments or points made throughout the speech — not word for word, but in a compressed, punchy way. This is to make sure the audience leaves with the core message firmly lodged in their minds.

2. It appeals emotionally. This is where the speaker turns up the emotional heat. They may use vivid imagery, passionate language, rhythmic sentences, or a stirring call to action to move the audience — to make them feel something deeply enough to act on it, believe it, or remember it forever.

So in short, the peroration is where logic steps back slightly and emotional power steps forward. It is the climax and close of the speech, rolled into one.

Imagine a lawyer in a courtroom who has spent an hour presenting evidence and building a logical case. Then, in the final few minutes, they turn to the jury, slow down, lower their voice, and say something like:

"Ladies and gentlemen, you have heard the facts. You have seen the evidence. Now I ask you — what kind of world do we want to live in? A just one, or a silent one? The choice is in your hands."

That closing passage — emotional, summarizing, designed to move — is the peroration. It is the moment the speech stops being an argument and starts being an experience.

The word peroration can also be used more loosely and often with a hint of mockery. In everyday language, people sometimes use it to describe any long, pompous, overly elaborate speech — the kind where someone goes on and on in a grand, self-important way without really saying much.

For example: "We had to sit through the chairman's usual peroration before the meeting could begin."

Here, the word carries a slightly sarcastic tone, implying the speech was more about the speaker showing off than actually communicating something valuable.

So while the primary meaning is neutral and technical (the conclusion of a speech), the secondary meaning is slightly critical — a bloated, showy speech.
How to Know Which Meaning Is Being Used

Context is your guide. If the word is used in a discussion about rhetoric, public speaking, or formal oratory, it almost certainly refers to the concluding section of a speech. If it's used in casual conversation about a person who tends to ramble grandly, it likely carries the mocking tone of the second meaning.

• A peroration is the ending of a formal speech, not just any ending — it is deliberate, crafted, and purposeful.
  • It typically summarizes and appeals emotionally, often at the same time.
  • It is the part of a speech designed to leave a mark — to make the audience feel, remember, and act.
  • In looser, more casual use, it can describe any long-winded, grand, pompous speech.
  • The word lives in the world of formal speaking and rhetoric, so you'll encounter it most often in discussions of oratory, politics, law, and literature.
11977:
"Perp" is simply a short, informal form of the word "perpetrator." A perpetrator is a person who commits a crime or does something seriously wrong or harmful. So a perp is, in plain terms, the person who did it — the one who carried out the bad act.

Think of it this way: if a robbery happens, the perp is the one who robbed. If a car is vandalized, the perp is the one who vandalized it. The word always points to a specific individual who is responsible for the wrongdoing.
Where You Will Hear This Word

"Perp" belongs to the world of law enforcement and crime. It is the everyday, shorthand language used by:

  • Police officers and detectives talking among themselves
  • Journalists and news reporters covering crime stories
  • Crime dramas and TV shows (you will hear it constantly in shows like Law & Order)
  • Everyday people when casually talking about crime

It is an informal, spoken word. You will not find it in a formal court document or a legal textbook. There, the proper word "perpetrator," or more precise legal terms like "defendant" or "the accused," would be used instead.
A Crucial Distinction: Guilt vs. Suspicion

This is important and often overlooked. The word "perp" carries an implicit assumption of guilt. When someone is called a perp, the speaker is treating it as more or less settled that this person did the crime. This is different from words like "suspect," which only means someone is believed to possibly have done it, without certainty.

In practice, police and reporters sometimes use "perp" loosely even before guilt is proven in court — which is technically not accurate from a legal standpoint, but it happens in informal speech all the time. As a learner of the word, just know: calling someone a perp is a stronger, more accusatory label than calling them a suspect.

You will very often see "perp" in the compound phrase "perp walk." This refers to the moment when police escort an arrested person — in handcuffs — in a visible, public way, often in front of waiting cameras and press. It is a well-known ritual in American crime culture and media. The arrested person is literally walked for all to see. The phrase is used both as a noun ("they did a perp walk") and a verb ("they perp-walked him out of the building").

"Perp" is not reserved for only big or violent crimes. It can refer to the person behind any kind of crime or wrongdoing — a pickpocket, a fraudster, a murderer, or a hacker. The word itself doesn't tell you how serious the crime was; it just tells you that this person is the one who did it.

In casual, everyday conversation, people sometimes use "perp" jokingly for situations that aren't actual crimes. For example: "Who ate the last slice of pizza? Find the perp!" Here it's being used in a playful, exaggerated way, borrowing the serious tone of crime language for comic effect. This kind of use is very common in informal speech.

• "The detective said they already had the perp in custody."
  • "Witnesses helped police identify the perp from a lineup."
  • "The news cameras were ready for the perp walk outside the courthouse."
  • "They caught the perp within 24 hours of the robbery."
Perp = the person who committed the crime. It's informal, it implies guilt, and it lives in the language of police, news, and crime storytelling.
11978:
To perpetrate something means to carry out or commit an act — almost always one that is wrong, harmful, illegal, or morally bad.

When you say someone perpetrated something, you are saying that they are the one who did it — they are directly responsible for making that bad thing happen.

Think of it this way: perpetrate = to be the one who does something bad.
The Most Important Thing to Understand About This Word

"Perpetrate" is not a neutral word. You would almost never use it to describe something good or ordinary. It carries a strong sense that the action is serious, deliberate, and wrong.

You perpetrate a crime. You perpetrate a fraud. You perpetrate an act of violence. You perpetrate a hoax. The word signals right away that something harmful or dishonest has been done — and that someone is to blame for it.

This is what makes it different from a simple word like "do" or "carry out." If you say "he did something," that's neutral. But if you say "he perpetrated something," you're immediately telling the listener: this was bad, and he is the one responsible.

Another key detail: perpetrating something almost always implies that the act was intentional — not an accident. The person chose to do it. They planned it, or at least consciously carried it out. This is why the word is so strongly connected to crimes and wrongdoing, where the question of who chose to do this matters enormously.
Who Is the Person Who Perpetrates?

The person who perpetrates an act is called the perpetrator. You will hear this word constantly in crime news, legal settings, and police reports. "The perpetrator fled the scene." "Investigators are searching for the perpetrator."

The act itself — the thing that was perpetrated — can be referred to as a perpetration, though this noun form is less common in everyday use.
The Register: When and Where This Word Is Used

"Perpetrate" is a formal word. You are far more likely to encounter it in:

  • News reports — "The attackers perpetrated one of the worst bombings in the city's history."
  • Legal and courtroom language — "The defendant perpetrated this act of fraud over several years."
  • Historical or academic writing — "The regime perpetrated widespread human rights abuses."

You would rarely hear it in casual everyday conversation. A friend wouldn't say, "Who perpetrated this mess in the kitchen?" — that would sound odd and overly dramatic. In normal speech, people would just say "did" or "committed."

Here are the kinds of acts most commonly used with this verb:

  • perpetrate a crime
  • perpetrate fraud / a scam
  • perpetrate violence
  • perpetrate a massacre or atrocity
  • perpetrate a hoax or deception
  • perpetrate abuse

Notice the pattern — these are all acts where someone causes serious harm or engages in serious dishonesty.

Here are clear, natural examples showing the word in action:

  1. "The gang perpetrated a series of bank robberies across three states."
  2. "He was convicted of perpetrating one of the largest financial frauds in history."
  3. "The investigation revealed that the attacks had been perpetrated by a small extremist group."
  4. "She perpetrated an elaborate hoax, fooling thousands of people online."
  5. "Those who perpetrate violence against civilians must be held accountable."
A Small Note on Humorous Use

Occasionally, writers use "perpetrate" in a lighthearted, ironic way to describe something minor — like a terrible joke or a bad pun. For example: "Who perpetrated this awful pun?" This works because the word's serious tone creates a funny contrast when applied to something harmless. But this is a stylistic trick, not the word's primary use. As a learner, focus first on the serious, formal meaning, and you'll understand the joke when you encounter it.

WordNuance

Several words are close in meaning but differ in subtle ways:

Commit is the most common everyday alternative — "to commit a crime" — and it works in both formal and informal settings. "Perpetrate" is more formal and often signals greater gravity or seriousness than "commit."

Carry out simply means to execute or perform an action, and it can be used for neutral things too ("carry out a plan"). "Perpetrate" cannot be used neutrally.

Conduct is often used for organized or systematic wrongdoing in formal contexts ("to conduct illegal experiments"), but it lacks the strong "blame" implication that "perpetrate" carries.
If you ever need to recall this word instantly: "perpetrate" means to deliberately commit a harmful or criminal act, and using this word points the finger directly at the person who did it.
11979:
A perpetrator is a person who commits a harmful, wrong, or illegal act. In the simplest terms: if something bad happened, the perpetrator is the one who did it.

Think of it this way — whenever there is a crime, an attack, abuse, a scam, or any serious wrongdoing, there is always a person behind it. That person is the perpetrator.
What Kind of Acts Does a Perpetrator Commit?

This word is used for a wide range of harmful actions, not just one specific type. A perpetrator can be:

  • The person who commits a murder or robbery
  • The person who carries out a terrorist attack
  • The person who commits fraud or financial crimes
  • The person who abuses someone physically, emotionally, or sexually
  • The person responsible for a massacre or large-scale atrocity

The common thread is always the same: a perpetrator is the doer of something harmful or wrong. The act doesn't always have to be illegal in the legal sense — it can also be deeply immoral or damaging. However, in everyday usage, you will almost always see this word used for serious wrongdoing.

Any person — regardless of gender, age, or background — can be called a perpetrator if they commit a harmful act. The word itself tells you nothing about who the person is beyond the fact that they did something wrong. It is a neutral label for the actor behind a bad deed.

It can also be used in the plural. When a crime or harmful act is carried out by a group of people, all of them together are called perpetrators.
The Register: Where and When Is This Word Used?

"Perpetrator" is a formal word. You will most commonly encounter it in:

  • News reports — journalists use it to describe the person responsible for a crime or attack without always naming them.
  • Legal and courtroom language — it is used to refer to the person who committed an offense.
  • Police and law enforcement contexts — officers and investigators use it when discussing crimes.
  • Academic and research writing — especially in fields like criminology, psychology, and sociology when studying harmful behavior.

It can be shortened to "perp" in informal police and detective language (you'll often hear this in crime dramas or thrillers), but in formal writing, the full word is always used.
An Important Nuance: Perpetrator vs. Suspect

These two words are often confused because they both appear in crime-related contexts, but they mean very different things.

A suspect is someone who is believed or thought to have committed the act — but it hasn't been proven yet. A perpetrator is the person who actually did it. So until guilt is established, the correct word is "suspect." Once the act is confirmed and a person is identified as the one who did it, "perpetrator" becomes appropriate.

This is why in careful journalism and legal language, you'll often see phrases like "the alleged perpetrator" — the word "alleged" signals that the person is being treated as the perpetrator but it has not yet been fully confirmed or proven in court.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding how "perpetrator" sits among related words will sharpen your grasp of it.

Criminal refers specifically to someone who has broken the law. Every criminal can be called a perpetrator, but not every perpetrator is necessarily a criminal in the strictly legal sense (for example, someone can perpetrate a moral wrong that isn't technically illegal).

Offender is very close in meaning and is also used in legal contexts. It tends to focus on the fact that someone has violated a rule or law. "Perpetrator" places more emphasis on the act itself — the person who carried out the harmful deed.

Culprit is a less formal word for the person responsible for something wrong or bad. It can be used for minor things too (like "Who's the culprit who ate the last slice of cake?"). "Perpetrator," by contrast, is almost always used for serious harm.

Wrongdoer is a general, somewhat old-fashioned word for anyone who does wrong. It's broader and softer in tone. "Perpetrator" is more precise and carries more weight and severity.

Here are the most natural and frequent ways this word appears in real language:

  • "The perpetrator fled the scene." — the person who committed the act escaped.
  • "Police are searching for the perpetrator." — the responsible person hasn't been caught yet.
  • "The perpetrators were sentenced to prison." — multiple people who committed the act were punished.
  • "The alleged perpetrator has been arrested." — the person suspected of doing it is in custody, but guilt isn't yet proven.
  • "Victims and perpetrators" — a common pairing used in discussions of crime, abuse, or conflict.
  • "The perpetrators of the attack" — those who carried out a specific harmful event.

Here are clear examples showing the word used naturally in different contexts:

"The security footage helped police identify the perpetrator of the robbery."

"Investigators are still working to determine whether the perpetrators acted alone or as part of a larger group."

"The report highlighted the need for better support systems for both victims and perpetrators of domestic abuse."

"Despite months of investigation, the perpetrator of the cyberattack has not been found."

"The court heard that the perpetrator had planned the crime several weeks in advance."

If you want to remember the word in one sentence: A perpetrator is the person who commits a harmful or wrongful act. Everything else about this word — its formal tone, its serious contexts, its relationship to words like "suspect" and "criminal" — builds on and surrounds that simple, solid core.
